boundaries.reason: This is a definition of observation maps, not a theorem about a sample with no subjects.
The event and censor times may equal zero, but no proof phase or zero-case property is asserted.
The definition applies to any sample size and asserts no singleton-sample result.
This definition does not prove existence or properties of a degenerate observation law.

boundaries.evidence: The Definition fixes event ties by T≤C, interval endpoints by L<T≤R, and strict truncation by T>L and T<R.
The Definition explicitly cites AC for the conditional-independence convention; its kernel versions are specified or supplied under the cited standard-Borel results.

The forward boundary therefore concerns the stated conditional calculation, not a two-way characterization.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed the entire Definition, seven direct prerequisite statements and the RCD/factorization proofs, and reader/refuter evidence. T and C are finite nonnegative Borel random elements; Z is standard Borel. Kernel existence invokes AC with nonempty standard-Borel targets; specified kernels have everywhere probability sections and parameter-specific almost-sure conditional identities. The measurable min/status maps assign ties to events; left/current-status censoring includes equality, intervals are (L,R], delayed entry is T>L and right truncation T<R. Zero times and deterministic thresholds are admissible. Independence and parameter-distinct endpoint laws are assumptions, with no converse/empirical-identification claim. Yu §§1.2.2 and 1.3 and Tian §2.1 confirm the observation conventions; Lin slide 95 agrees for continuous laws but uses weak right truncation, whereas this definition explicitly fixes strict truncation. No defect or new choice use found.

citations.quote:
An **event time** is a measurable real-valued map $T$ with values in $[0,\infty)$. A **covariate** is a measurable map $Z$ into a specified standard-Borel space $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal B)$, where standard Borel means measurably isomorphic to a Polish space ([[def-standard-borel-space]]). A **censoring or inspection time** is a measurable real-valued map $C$ with values in $[0,\infty)$. When conditional laws are used, they are probability kernels $K_T(z,\cdot)$ and $K_C(z,\cdot)$ in the sense of [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]] and [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. They are part of the specified model; their existence for real-valued targets and factorization through standard-Borel $Z$ follow under [[def-axiom-of-choice]] from [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]] and [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]].

The notation $T\perp\!\!\!\perp C\mid\sigma(Z)$ has the meaning in [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]: for bounded measurable $a,b$, $\mathbb E[a(T)b(C)\mid\sigma(Z)]=\mathbb E[a(T)\mid\sigma(Z)]\mathbb E[b(C)\mid\sigma(Z)]$ almost surely. It is a model assumption about the conditional observation law, not a consequence of adjusting for $Z$ and not an empirical conclusion.

Under **right censoring**, the recorded pair is $U=\min(T,C)$ and $\delta=1\{T\le C\}$. Thus $\delta=1$ records an event at $U=T$, including a tie, while $\delta=0$ records censoring at $U=C$ and implies $T>C$. **Left censoring** at a known threshold $L$ records only $T\le L$. **Interval censoring** at known endpoints $L<R$ records $L<T\le R$. **Current-status observation** at an inspection time $C$ records only $\delta_C=1\{T\le C\}$.

**Left truncation**, also called delayed entry at $L$, selects a unit into the sample only when $T>L$; observation begins after that selection. **Right truncation** at $R$ selects a unit only when $T<R$. These are selection rules before the observed sample is formed, whereas censoring coarsens an event time after sampling. The strict and weak inequalities in these definitions fix the endpoint conventions. A random observation endpoint is called noninformative here only when it is fixed by design or is generated independently of $T$ conditional on the stated covariates under a parameter-distinct law; otherwise its joint observation law must be modeled.

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

Let
$$\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). When the model is
parametric, write $\mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). A **scientific statistical model
contract** is an explicit record of the following fields for a specified
analysis.

1. **Observation space and record.** Give $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and say
   which values form one recorded data object. A response and each predictor
   used as a function of the data must be a specified measurable map from this
   space to a named measurable target. This is the map convention for a
   statistic in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]; it does not make a predictor
   causal or the response law correct.

2. **Scientific, sampling, assignment, and analysis units.** Name the
   biological or physical unit about which the scientific question is asked,
   the sample unit selected for observation when sampling occurs, the
   assignment unit receiving a randomized treatment when randomization occurs,
   and the analysis unit represented in each data record. These roles may
   differ. A technical replicate is a repeated reading or assay of the same
   specimen; a biological replicate is a distinct biological unit. Neither
   term asserts independence. State whether enrollment is a probability
   sample or a specified convenience/design cohort.

3. **Indices and time.** Give every unit, treatment, visit, and repeated
   measurement index, the object each index identifies, and the time origin.
   In particular, do not identify a participant index with a visit or assay
   index merely because all are written as rows in a data array.

4. **Quantity status.** Mark each model quantity as **fixed** (held
   nonrandom under the declared law), **random** (a measurable random element
   with its law specified, using [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]
   and [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]), **observed** (recorded
   in the data object), or **latent** (part of a fuller model state but not
   recorded). A latent quantity must separately be declared fixed or random.
   If inference conditions on a design value or event, name it and state the
   conditional law being used.

5. **Target and estimand.** Name the target population of units, settings,
   and time period, and distinguish it from the enrolled or observed sample.
   Specify the target as a function $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T$ when it is an
   estimand in the parametric model, as in
   [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]. The contract alone does not show
   that the target is identifiable. Identifiability means that equality of
   sampling laws forces equality of target values
   ([[def-identifiability-of-an-estimand]]).

6. **Observation mechanism.** State how a fuller scientific state becomes
   the recorded data. A deterministic mechanism is a specified measurable map
   $O:(\mathcal W,\mathcal G)\to(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. A stochastic
   mechanism is specified by $K:\mathcal W\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ such that,
   for each $w$, $A\mapsto K(w,A)$ is a probability measure and, for each
   $A\in\mathcal A$, $w\mapsto K(w,A)$ is measurable. These clauses define the
   mechanism supplied by the contract; they do not assert that a conditional
   version exists for an arbitrary joint law.

7. **Support and law.** State the sampling law $P_\theta$ on
   $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. For an asserted support set, give a measurable
   $S_\theta\subseteq\mathcal X$ with $P_\theta(S_\theta)=1$. If “support”
   instead means topological support, name the topology and the conditions
   under which that convention is being used. If densities are used, name the
   dominating measure and state whether their positive sets agree across
   parameter values. For a randomized design, also state its assignment law;
   if inference averages over assignments, give the resulting joint law.

8. **Conditioning convention.** Say whether inference uses the joint law,
   averaging over the declared randomization, or a specified conditional law
   given the realized design. A conditional law at an event of probability
   zero must be supplied as a specified version with its existence
   hypotheses; it is not defined by an ordinary probability ratio.

9. **Adequacy assumptions.** List each scientific adequacy assumption and
   classify it as **design-controlled** (imposed by protocol and checked
   against implementation records), **empirically assessable** (data or
   validation measurements can challenge it, without proving it true), or
   **substantively untestable** from the declared observed-data law (external
   domain evidence or additional assumptions are needed). Split an assumption
   that has different parts into separate entries and justify each label.

These are bookkeeping and interpretation requirements. They do not assert that
an empirical law equals a proposed model, that a design was implemented as
specified, that calibration is valid, or that any scientific or physical
application is adequate. No independence, exchangeability, missingness,
causal-identification, or common-support assumption follows from the indexing
or the classification labels. This definition uses no axiom of choice.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ and $Y:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\mathcal T)$ be measurable random elements. A **conditional law of X given Y** is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that $\omega\mapsto K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$ in [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. Thus for every $A\in\mathcal S$ and $H\in\sigma(Y)$,
$$\int_H K(Y(\omega),A)\,dP=P(H\cap\{X\in A\}).$$

Composition with Y makes each evaluation $\sigma(Y)$-measurable, and every section remains a probability by [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. The notation $P(X\in A\mid Y=y)=K(y,A)$ refers to a chosen kernel; it is not a ratio involving the possibly zero probability $P(Y=y)$.

Write $P_Y(B)=P(Y^{-1}(B))$ for the law in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. If a specified countable family $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S$ determines probability measures, two conditional laws K,L agree as measures outside a single $\mathcal T$-measurable $P_Y$-null set. Indeed for each $A\in\mathcal C$ the measurable discrepancy $D_A=\{y:K(y,A)\ne L(y,A)\}$ has null inverse image under Y by [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]]. Hence $P_Y(D_A)=0$ by the law definition; the countable union $D$ is null by [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]], and off D the determining property gives equality of measures. This uses a supplied determining family and makes no AC assertion about obtaining one.

Values on a measurable $P_Y$-null subset may be replaced by a specified fixed probability on E without changing these identities. The inverse image of that subset is measurable null, and all event evaluations are bounded, so the modified event integrals agree. Empty-event evaluations remain zero and whole-target evaluations remain one. Existence on standard-Borel spaces is proved separately; the definition alone does not assert a conditional kernel exists.

Assume AC. Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable random element with standard-Borel target, and let $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be any sub-sigma-algebra. There exists a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\mathcal G$. Every section is a probability measure, including at exceptional sample points, and no countable-generation or completeness assumption on $\mathcal G$ is required.

For this necessarily nonempty target, the construction also supplies a bimeasurable bijection $c:E\to B$ onto a Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$, and a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures.

Assume AC. Let $X$ and $Y$ take values in nonempty standard-Borel spaces $(E,\mathcal S)$ and $(T,\mathcal T)$ on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$. Let $L$ be a specified regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$, everywhere a probability kernel. There is a probability kernel $K:T\to E$ such that $L(\omega,\cdot)=K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ simultaneously outside a single null set. In fact, with the stated everywhere-kernel convention, the construction below gives this equality for every $\omega$. Consequently K is a conditional law of X given Y.

Assume the axiom of choice so that the library's conditional-expectation
classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,
$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$
This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on
representatives.

For sigma-algebras $\mathcal H_1,\mathcal H_2\subseteq\mathcal F$, the notation
$\mathcal H_1\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal H_2\mid\mathcal G$ means the same identity
for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded
$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

The definition is symmetric. If $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ modulo
null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that
factor is already known when conditioning. The choices of the zero function or
the constant-one function cause no exceptional case.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $\mu$ be a Borel measure on $\mathbb{R}$ finite on compact sets. Its
**distribution function normalized at $0$** is the function
$F_\mu : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by

$$F_\mu(x) := \begin{cases} \mu((0,x]), & x \ge 0,\\ -\mu((x,0]), & x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Both interval measures are finite: the relevant half-open interval is
contained in the closed bounded interval with endpoints $0$ and $x$, which is
compact by [[thm-heine-borel-r]], and measure monotonicity
[[prop-measure-monotonicity]] applies.

The two cases agree at $x = 0$, where both give $0$. This normalization removes
the additive-constant ambiguity that would remain if one used only interval
increments.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $\mu$ be a Borel measure on
$\mathbb{R}$ finite on compact sets, and let
$F_\mu$ be its normalized distribution function from
[[def-distribution-function-of-a-borel-measure-on-r]]. Then:

1. $F_\mu$ is nondecreasing and right-continuous;
2. for every $a < b$,

   $$F_\mu(b) - F_\mu(a) = \mu((a,b]);$$

3. the Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure attached to $F_\mu$ is exactly $\mu$.

Conversely, if $F,G : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ are nondecreasing and
right-continuous, then $\mu_F = \mu_G$ if and only if $F-G$ is constant on
$\mathbb{R}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let
$F : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be nondecreasing and right-continuous, and let
$\mu_F$ be its Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure. Then for every $a < b$,

$$\mu_F((a,b)) = F(b^-) - F(a),$$

$$\mu_F([a,b]) = F(b) - F(a^-),$$

$$\mu_F([a,b)) = F(b^-) - F(a^-),$$

and

$$\mu_F(\{a\}) = F(a) - F(a^-).$$

Consequently $a$ is an atom of $\mu_F$ in the sense of
[[def-atom-of-a-measure-on-r]] if and only if $F(a) > F(a^-)$, and the set of
atoms of $\mu_F$ is at most countable.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For fixed entry, the event kernel given the pre-entry covariates $W$ is $K^T_\theta(W,\cdot)$. For random entry, the stated factorization of the pre-entry conditional joint law gives the same event kernel given $Z=(W,L)$ before selection. In either case, conditional on $Z$ and the positive-probability inclusion event $T>L$, the event law assigns a set $A$ probability $K^T_\theta(W,A\cap(L,\infty))/S_\theta(L\mid W)$. Conditional independence of $T$ and $C$ given $Z$ means restricting their product law to $T>L$ leaves this truncated event law and the same censor law as a product. The event density is therefore $f_\theta(u\mid W)/S_\theta(L\mid W)$ for $u>L$, and the conditional survivor is $S_\theta(u\mid W)/S_\theta(L\mid W)$ for every $u\ge L$; at $u=L$ this equals $1$, including when the censoring law has an atom at entry. Applying the branch calculations from steps 3.1–4.1 under that product law yields the asserted denominator, once, in either event-status branch.

Every factorization above was conditional on the stated independence, domination, endpoint, and positivity assumptions. The calculations give no evidence that a real censoring, inspection, or entry mechanism satisfies them; an informative mechanism requires its own joint law.

An **event time** is a measurable real-valued map $T$ with values in $[0,\infty)$. A **covariate** is a measurable map $Z$ into a specified standard-Borel space $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal B)$, where standard Borel means measurably isomorphic to a Polish space ([[def-standard-borel-space]]). A **censoring or inspection time** is a measurable real-valued map $C$ with values in $[0,\infty)$. When conditional laws are used, they are probability kernels $K_T(z,\cdot)$ and $K_C(z,\cdot)$ in the sense of [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]] and [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. They are part of the specified model; their existence for real-valued targets and factorization through standard-Borel $Z$ follow under [[def-axiom-of-choice]] from [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]] and [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]].

The notation $T\perp\!\!\!\perp C\mid\sigma(Z)$ has the meaning in [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]: for bounded measurable $a,b$, $\mathbb E[a(T)b(C)\mid\sigma(Z)]=\mathbb E[a(T)\mid\sigma(Z)]\mathbb E[b(C)\mid\sigma(Z)]$ almost surely. It is a model assumption about the conditional observation law, not a consequence of adjusting for $Z$ and not an empirical conclusion.

Under **right censoring**, the recorded pair is $U=\min(T,C)$ and $\delta=1\{T\le C\}$. Thus $\delta=1$ records an event at $U=T$, including a tie, while $\delta=0$ records censoring at $U=C$ and implies $T>C$. **Left censoring** at a known threshold $L$ records only $T\le L$. **Interval censoring** at known endpoints $L<R$ records $L<T\le R$. **Current-status observation** at an inspection time $C$ records only $\delta_C=1\{T\le C\}$.

**Left truncation**, also called delayed entry at $L$, selects a unit into the sample only when $T>L$; observation begins after that selection. **Right truncation** at $R$ selects a unit only when $T<R$. These are selection rules before the observed sample is formed, whereas censoring coarsens an event time after sampling. The strict and weak inequalities in these definitions fix the endpoint conventions. A random observation endpoint is called noninformative here only when it is fixed by design or is generated independently of $T$ conditional on the stated covariates under a parameter-distinct law; otherwise its joint observation law must be modeled.

derivations.claim: In Model A, the outcome $T=1$ has probability $1/2$ and gives $(U,\delta)=(1,1)$ because $C=4$. The outcome $T=3$ has probability $1/2$ and gives $(U,\delta)=(1/2,0)$ because $C=1/2<T$.
In Model B, $T=1$ again gives $(U,\delta)=(1,1)$ with probability $1/2$, while $T=2$ gives $(U,\delta)=(1/2,0)$ with probability $1/2$.
For the truncation example, $P(T>1)=\int_1^3(1/3)\,dt=2/3$.
Both observed laws assign probability $1/2$ to each of $(1,1)$ and $(1/2,0)$, although the censoring time is a deterministic function of $T$ in each model.

Conditional on inclusion, the event-time density is $(1/3)/(2/3)=1/2$ on $(1,3)$ and zero outside, whereas the unselected density is $1/3$ on $(0,3)$. Thus left truncation changes the sampled event-time law.
The event-time laws differ: $P_A(T\le2)=1/2$ and $P_B(T\le2)=1$. Equal observed laws with different event-time laws contradict the refuted statement.

The finite censoring construction refutes the claim about equal observed laws, and the uniform calculation shows that truncation changes the sampling distribution by selection. Informative censoring requires its joint observation law to be modeled.

An **event time** is a measurable real-valued map $T$ with values in $[0,\infty)$. A **covariate** is a measurable map $Z$ into a specified standard-Borel space $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal B)$, where standard Borel means measurably isomorphic to a Polish space ([[def-standard-borel-space]]). A **censoring or inspection time** is a measurable real-valued map $C$ with values in $[0,\infty)$. When conditional laws are used, they are probability kernels $K_T(z,\cdot)$ and $K_C(z,\cdot)$ in the sense of [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]] and [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. They are part of the specified model; their existence for real-valued targets and factorization through standard-Borel $Z$ follow under [[def-axiom-of-choice]] from [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]] and [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]].

The notation $T\perp\!\!\!\perp C\mid\sigma(Z)$ has the meaning in [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]: for bounded measurable $a,b$, $\mathbb E[a(T)b(C)\mid\sigma(Z)]=\mathbb E[a(T)\mid\sigma(Z)]\mathbb E[b(C)\mid\sigma(Z)]$ almost surely. It is a model assumption about the conditional observation law, not a consequence of adjusting for $Z$ and not an empirical conclusion.

Under **right censoring**, the recorded pair is $U=\min(T,C)$ and $\delta=1\{T\le C\}$. Thus $\delta=1$ records an event at $U=T$, including a tie, while $\delta=0$ records censoring at $U=C$ and implies $T>C$. **Left censoring** at a known threshold $L$ records only $T\le L$. **Interval censoring** at known endpoints $L<R$ records $L<T\le R$. **Current-status observation** at an inspection time $C$ records only $\delta_C=1\{T\le C\}$.

**Left truncation**, also called delayed entry at $L$, selects a unit into the sample only when $T>L$; observation begins after that selection. **Right truncation** at $R$ selects a unit only when $T<R$. These are selection rules before the observed sample is formed, whereas censoring coarsens an event time after sampling. The strict and weak inequalities in these definitions fix the endpoint conventions. A random observation endpoint is called noninformative here only when it is fixed by design or is generated independently of $T$ conditional on the stated covariates under a parameter-distinct law; otherwise its joint observation law must be modeled.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $Z,T,C$ be random elements, with $Z$ taking values in a standard-Borel space ([[def-standard-borel-space]]) and $T,C$ taking values in $[0,\infty)$ with its Borel sigma-algebra. Consider the conditional experiment given the observed covariate $Z=z$. For each $(\theta,\eta)$ in a product parameter space $\Theta\times H$, let $K^T_\theta(z,\cdot)$ and $K^C_\eta(z,\cdot)$ be the specified conditional event-time and censor-time laws. Assume $T\perp\!\!\!\perp C\mid\sigma(Z)$ under each parameter pair. Assume $K^T_\theta(z,dt)=f_\theta(t\mid z)\,dt$ with a jointly measurable density in $(z,t)$, and that every $K^C_\eta(z,\cdot)$ is dominated by one fixed sigma-finite measure $\nu$ with a jointly measurable density $g_\eta(z,c)$. The event law depends only on $\theta$ and the censor law only on $\eta$. All displayed conditional identities hold for $P_{Z;\theta,\eta}$-almost every $z$ under each fixed parameter pair $(\theta,\eta)$, where $P_{Z;\theta,\eta}$ is the marginal law of $Z$ under that pair as in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. All density equalities are in their almost-everywhere versions for that pair; no common exceptional set over an uncountable parameter set is asserted.

For right-censored data $(U,\delta)$, define the reference measure $\rho$ on $[0,\infty)\times\{0,1\}$ by $\rho(B\times\{1\})=\operatorname{Leb}(B)$ and $\rho(B\times\{0\})=\nu(B)$. Put $S_\theta(u\mid z)=K^T_\theta(z,(u,\infty))$ and $G_\eta(u\mid z)=K^C_\eta(z,[u,\infty))$. In the scientific model contract of [[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]], one analysis unit is one subject; the full-data random quantities are $T,C$, and the observation map records $(Z,U,\delta)=(Z,\min(T,C),1\{T\le C\})$, so the record contains the minimum and status rather than both full times. This theorem conditions on observed $Z$ and asserts no target-population estimand or empirical adequacy. The conditional density of $(U,\delta)$ with respect to $\rho$ is

$$h_{\theta,\eta}(u,1\mid z)=f_\theta(u\mid z)G_\eta(u\mid z),\qquad h_{\theta,\eta}(u,0\mid z)=S_\theta(u\mid z)g_\eta(z,u).$$

Consequently, up to the censor-only factor, the event-model likelihood contribution is $f_\theta(U\mid Z)^\delta S_\theta(U\mid Z)^{1-\delta}$, where the two cases mean $f_\theta(U\mid Z)$ when $\delta=1$ and $S_\theta(U\mid Z)$ when $\delta=0$. This is a conditional likelihood given $Z$; a parameter-dependent marginal law of $Z$ would supply a separate factor.

For an arbitrary conditional event-time law $\mu_{\theta,z}$ on $[0,\infty)$ with distribution function $F_\theta(t\mid z)=\mu_{\theta,z}((-\infty,t])$, for $0\le L\le R<\infty$,

$$P(L<T\le R\mid Z=z)=F_\theta(R\mid z)-F_\theta(L\mid z),\qquad P(T\le L\mid Z=z)=F_\theta(L\mid z),$$

and $P(T=t\mid Z=z)=F_\theta(t\mid z)-F_\theta(t^-\mid z)$. For fixed inspection endpoints, or endpoints conditionally independent of $T$ given $Z$ under a law with no event parameter $\theta$, these are the event factors for interval and left-censored observations. In current-status observation at a fixed inspection time $c$, the event contribution is $F_\theta(c\mid z)^\delta S_\theta(c\mid z)^{1-\delta}$, with $S_\theta(c\mid z)=P(T>c\mid Z=z)$ and $\delta=1\{T\le c\}$. An informative inspection process requires its own joint model.

For delayed entry at $L$, let $W$ denote all pre-entry covariates; take $Z=W$ when $L$ is fixed by design and $Z=(W,L)$ when random $L$ is observed. In the random-entry case, assume that before selection the conditional joint law of $(T,L)$ given $W=w$ factors as $K^T_\theta(w,dt)Q_\eta(w,d\ell)$, where the entry kernel $Q_\eta$ does not depend on the event parameter $\theta$. Thus $L\perp\!\!\!\perp T\mid W$ under this parameter-distinct entry model, and the event law given $Z=(W,L)$ remains $K^T_\theta(W,\cdot)$. For each parameter pair, require $S_\theta(L\mid W)>0$ for almost every $(W,L)$ under its pre-selection law, select only units with $T>L$, and assume post-entry right censoring satisfies $T\perp\!\!\!\perp C\mid\sigma(Z)$ with $C\ge L$. Conditional on inclusion $T>L$, the event density and survivor terms are $f_\theta(u\mid W)/S_\theta(L\mid W)$ for an event and $S_\theta(u\mid W)/S_\theta(L\mid W)$ for censoring, for $u>L$. Thus the right-censored event contribution is divided by $S_\theta(L\mid W)$. An event branch has $u>L$, while a censoring branch may have $u=L$ when the censoring law has an atom at entry; the survivor ratio $S_\theta(u\mid W)/S_\theta(L\mid W)$ applies for every $u\ge L$.

For right truncation at fixed $R$, or at an observed threshold conditionally independent of $T$ given $Z$ under a law with no event parameter $\theta$, inclusion is conditional on $T<R$ with $P(T<R\mid Z=z)>0$. Its conditional event-time law is $\mu_{\theta,z}(A\cap(-\infty,R))/P(T<R\mid Z=z)$; in the continuous-density case the selected-sample density is $f_\theta(t\mid z)/F_\theta(R^-\mid z)$ for $t<R$. This selection likelihood is distinct from the right-censoring likelihood. Independence of censoring, inspection, or entry is a model assumption, not a theorem about an empirical study.

derivations.claim: Integrating the density gives $F_\lambda(t)=1-e^{-\lambda t}$ and $S_\lambda(t)=e^{-\lambda t}$ for $t\ge0$; in particular $F_\lambda(0)=0$ and $S_\lambda(0)=1$.

With fixed censoring time $C=2$, an event observed at $U=1$ has event factor $f_\lambda(1)=\lambda e^{-\lambda}$ and censor factor $1$. A censored observation at $U=2$ has event factor $S_\lambda(2)=e^{-2\lambda}$ and censor factor $1$ relative to the point-mass censoring law.
An interval observation $1<T\le2$ has probability $F_\lambda(2)-F_\lambda(1)=(1-e^{-2\lambda})-(1-e^{-\lambda})=e^{-\lambda}-e^{-2\lambda}$.
At fixed inspection time $C=1$, current status $\delta=1$ has event factor $F_\lambda(1)=1-e^{-\lambda}$, and $\delta=0$ has event factor $S_\lambda(1)=e^{-\lambda}$.

After delayed entry $L=1$, with fixed censoring time $C=3$, an event observed at $U=2$ has conditional event factor $f_\lambda(2)/S_\lambda(1)=\lambda e^{-2\lambda}/e^{-\lambda}=\lambda e^{-\lambda}$. A censored observation at $U=3$ has conditional event factor $S_\lambda(3)/S_\lambda(1)=e^{-2\lambda}$.

If instead the sample is right-truncated at $R=2$, the selected-sample density is $\lambda e^{-\lambda t}/(1-e^{-2\lambda})$ for $0\le t<2$, since $P(T<2)=F_\lambda(2)=1-e^{-2\lambda}$. This is a conditional event-time density, not a right-censoring contribution.

The censoring and truncation examples use different event factors: ordinary right censoring uses $f_\lambda(u)$ or $S_\lambda(u)$, delayed entry divides by $S_\lambda(1)$, and right truncation divides by $P(T<2)$.
